messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya Patel was 43 when a chemical exposure on a job site changed the way she moved through her days. She had been working as a plumber in the basement mechanical room of an older apartment building, tracing a leak near a water heater and a cluster of corroded pipes, when a sharp burnt odor began spreading through the enclosed space. At first she thought it was smoke from faulty wiring or an overheated motor. Within moments the smell thickened into something harsher and chemical, catching in her throat and nose. What stayed with her afterward was not only the fear that something toxic was in the air, but the particular sensory imprint of it: the burnt, smoky smell in a cramped work space where she could not immediately tell what was burning, where it was coming from, or whether another breath was dangerous.

In the weeks after, smells became the quickest route back into that moment. A faint smoke smell drifting from a neighboring yard, an acrid odor from a furnace room, even a vaguely burnt smell from a job involving old equipment could make Priya’s body react before she had time to think. Her chest tightened, her stomach dropped, and she found herself instantly on guard, scanning for exits, vents, scorch marks, anything that might confirm she was in danger again. At night she woke abruptly and alert, checking the house room by room or lying still and sniffing the air to make sure nothing toxic was leaking in while her husband slept. She had come to feel that her body was acting as if the threat were still present, and the stronger those jolts became, the more convincing it felt that she could not afford to relax.

Those reactions changed how she worked. Priya began checking every environment she entered with unusual intensity, especially basements, boiler rooms, and utility spaces where odd odors were common. Before kneeling to inspect a pipe she would pause and test the air, looking around for any sign of smoke, residue, or overheating. If a smell reminded her even remotely of that day, she pulled back emotionally as well as physically. She tried to flatten herself inside, avoiding not only fear but anything stirring at all, as if shutting down feeling might keep her from being overwhelmed. She also started refusing anything that brought her close to medical settings. She would not go into hospitals, grew tense at the sound or sight of ambulances, and put off physical examinations because those cues pulled too close to the possibility that the exposure had done unseen damage.

Over months, the habits that seemed protective made the smells loom larger. Because Priya was constantly sampling the air and watching for danger, she noticed burnt and smoky odors everywhere: a customer’s singed toast, a heater kicking on, traffic fumes near a service call. The more she checked, the more often she detected something that might mean risk. Avoiding medical cues left her with no reassuring way to test her fears, and her effort to avoid all feeling made the odors seem even more abrupt and intrusive when they broke through. She began taking longer routes through buildings to avoid certain hallways and mechanical rooms, and at work her delays became noticeable. A job that once would have been routine could stretch because she was standing still, listening, smelling, and searching for proof that the space was safe enough to enter.

Her hypervigilance also fed the problem in the other direction. Because she was already on edge, small smells registered as alarms. A trace of something burnt that other people dismissed as “nothing” hit her like evidence she had missed an active threat. When she woke in the night already alert, the ordinary smells of the house seemed charged and suspicious, and she would get up to check windows, appliances, and the hallway again. She was certain that letting her guard down would be the moment something serious happened. What frightened her most was not just another exposure, but the idea that her senses might fail her if she stopped monitoring.

By the time Priya sought help, her world had narrowed around smell, scanning, and exhaustion. Her husband had begun to comment on how often she was up at night checking the house, and she had started turning down plumbing jobs in settings where burnt or chemical odors were likely. She came in because she could see her work being affected and because she was tired of living as if every faint smoky smell meant immediate danger. At the same time, she was afraid that treatment might ask her to ignore signs she believed could save her life. What she hoped for, cautiously, was to be able to walk into a mechanical room and trust herself again without her body going instantly on high alert.
